title: Reverse Bits
directAnswer: Reverse the 32 bits of an unsigned integer. Build the answer one bit at a time: pull the lowest bit of the input with `n & 1`, append it to the result with `result = (result << 1) | bit`, then drop it from the input with an UNSIGNED shift. For repeated calls, cache reversed bytes and stitch four of them together.

remember.formula:
result = 0
for _ in range(32):
    result = (result << 1) | (n & 1)  # append low bit of n
    n >>= 1                            # drop it (unsigned in Java)
return result
rules: Mirror the two shifts: **read** the low bit of `n` (`n & 1`), **write** it to the low end of `result` (`result << 1 | bit`).
Always loop exactly **32** times — leading zeros of the input become trailing zeros of the output and must be preserved.
In Java use the **unsigned** shift `n >>>= 1`; `>>` sign-extends and corrupts the high bits of a negative input.
In Python, mask intermediates with **`& 0xFFFFFFFF`** when you right-shift or you'll carry an ever-growing arbitrary-precision int; the bit-by-bit *build* stays in range naturally.
Position `i` of the input maps to position `31 - i` of the output — that symmetry is the whole problem.
whenToUse: Reverse / mirror the bit order of a fixed-width integer
The function is called repeatedly → cache reversed bytes/nibbles
Any 'flip position i to position width-1-i' transformation
antiSignals: You only need to count bits, not reorder them → Brian Kernighan (Number of 1 Bits)
Reversing the decimal digits, not the binary bits → that's an integer-math problem, not bitwise
The width isn't fixed → 'reverse 32 bits' assumes exactly 32; a variable width changes the loop bound
You want individual bit access, not a full mirror → mask the specific position
remember.takeaway: Reverse Bits is the canonical 'consume from one end, build at the other' bit loop. The trap isn't the algorithm — it's unsigned handling: Java needs `>>>`, Python needs `& 0xFFFFFFFF` on shifts. Get the masking right and the rest is a 32-step mirror.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can manipulate bits at fixed positions and — critically — handle unsignedness correctly in a language without unsigned types (Java's signed int, Python's unbounded int).
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using a signed right shift in Java (corrupts negatives), stopping the loop early instead of a full 32 iterations (drops leading-zero handling), or in Python letting the int grow past 32 bits without masking.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the read-bit / write-bit symmetry, state that position i maps to 31 - i, handle unsigned correctly without prompting, and offer the byte-cache optimisation for the 'called many times' follow-up.

problemStatement:
Reverse the bits of a given 32-bit **unsigned** integer.

Note: in some languages (such as Java) there is no unsigned integer type, so the input and output are given as signed integers — they should not affect your implementation, as the internal binary representation is the same whether signed or unsigned.

Follow-up: if this function is called **many times**, how would you optimize it?
constraints: The input is a 32-bit unsigned integer
In Java the value is given as a signed int (same bit pattern)
Follow-up: optimize for many repeated calls (caching)
understanding: Take a 32-bit number and produce the number whose binary digits are in the exact reverse order — bit at position 0 goes to position 31, bit 1 to bit 30, and so on. Leading zeros matter: they become trailing zeros after the flip, so the width is fixed at 32.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the width fixed at 32 bits?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That matters because leading zeros must be reversed too — a 1 at position 0 must land at position 31 even if the higher bits are all zero.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How do I handle the lack of unsigned ints in Java?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Use the unsigned right shift `>>>` when consuming bits so the sign bit doesn't propagate. The 32-bit pattern is identical regardless of signedness.

clarifyingQuestions.question: In Python, won't the integer grow beyond 32 bits?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Python ints are arbitrary-precision. The bit-by-bit build naturally stays within 32 bits, but if I right-shift a wider value I mask with & 0xFFFFFFFF to stay in the 32-bit window.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Will this be called repeatedly?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The follow-up says yes. Then I'd precompute reversed bytes (256-entry table) and reverse the number by reversing and reordering its four bytes.

examples.explanation: Reading the input right-to-left gives the output left-to-right — the bit string is mirrored.
Only bit 1 is 0; after reversal that 0 sits at position 30. All-ones-but-one flips to all-ones-but-one on the other side.
The single set bit at position 0 moves to position 31. Demonstrates why all 32 iterations matter.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Bit-by-bit is the clean default; the byte cache wins when the function is hammered repeatedly.

approaches.name: Bit-by-Bit — Shift In, Shift Out
approaches.whenToMention: The clean default everyone should produce first. 'Pop the low bit of n, push it onto result, repeat 32 times.'
hints: If you read the input's bits from the lowest upward, and write them into the result from the lowest upward, what order does the result end up in?
Each step: take the lowest bit of n (n & 1), and append it to result by shifting result left and OR-ing the bit in.
Then shift n right (UNSIGNED in Java) to expose the next bit. Do this exactly 32 times so leading zeros are placed too.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Exactly 32 iterations of constant-time bit ops regardless of input, so O(1) time. Only the result accumulator is stored — O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Build the answer bit by bit. Each iteration: read the lowest bit of `n` with `n & 1`, shift `result` left by one to open a slot, OR the bit into that slot, then shift `n` right to expose the next bit. After 32 iterations the bits have been transferred in mirror order.

**Why the two shifts mirror each other.** You consume `n` from its *low* end (`n & 1` then `n >>= 1`) and you grow `result` at its *low* end (`result << 1 | bit`). The first bit you read becomes the most significant bit of `result` because it gets shifted left 31 more times as later bits arrive. That is precisely the position-`i` → position-`31 - i` mapping the problem asks for.

**Why exactly 32 iterations, never early-exit.** If you stop when `n` becomes `0`, you skip the input's leading zeros — but those zeros must become trailing zeros in the output, and equivalently the set bits they precede must be shifted to their correct high positions. Running the full 32 steps guarantees every bit, including zeros, lands where it belongs. Example: `n = 1` needs all 32 left-shifts of `result` to push that single bit to position 31.

**Why unsigned shifts matter.** In Java, `n >>= 1` on a negative value copies the sign bit downward, injecting phantom 1s and corrupting the reversal. `n >>>= 1` pulls in `0`, treating the value as the unsigned 32-bit pattern the problem specifies. In Python the *build* never exceeds 32 bits, but if you shift a wider intermediate you mask with `& 0xFFFFFFFF` to clamp back into the 32-bit window.
approaches.insight: Reversal is just two coordinated queues: you dequeue bits from the bottom of `n` and enqueue them onto the bottom of `result`. Because `result` keeps shifting left, the earliest-dequeued bit floats to the top — a stack/queue intuition expressed in pure bit ops.

dryRun.intro: Read low bit of n, append to result, shift both. Watch the first bit read rise to the top.

steps.action: n is 0; result keeps shifting left, appending 0s
steps.note: the 29 extra shifts place the bits at the top — why we run all 32

dryRun.result: 0b101 reversed within 32 bits → 1010...0 (bit that was at pos 0 is now at pos 31)

java.explanation: Open a low slot in result (<<1) and drop in n's current lowest bit (n & 1).
UNSIGNED shift: expose the next bit without sign-extending. Plain >> would inject 1s on a negative input.

python.explanation: Append n's lowest bit to the bottom of result; earlier bits float upward.
Drop the consumed bit. n is non-negative here so no mask is needed on the input side.

diagrams.title: First bit read becomes the top bit
diagrams.caption: Reading from n's low end and writing to result's low end mirrors the bit order.

edgeCases.behavior: Every bit read is 0; result stays 0 through all 32 shifts → returns 0.
All 32 bits are 1; with >>> each is read and re-placed → returns -1 (0xFFFFFFFF). With >> the loop would still read 1s but on a single sign-extended value.

pitfalls: Using >> instead of >>> in Java — corrupts the high bits of a negative input.
Stopping the loop when n == 0 — drops leading zeros and leaves set bits at the wrong positions.
In Python, right-shifting a value wider than 32 bits without `& 0xFFFFFFFF` — lets the int grow unbounded.

approaches.name: Byte Cache — Reverse and Reorder Bytes (Optimal for Repeated Calls)
approaches.whenToMention: The follow-up answer for 'called many times'. 'Precompute reversed bytes once; each call reverses 4 bytes and swaps their order.'
hints: If you'll reverse millions of numbers, what work can you do ONCE and reuse? A 32-bit int is just 4 bytes.
Reversing the whole number = reverse each of the 4 bytes individually, then put the bytes in the opposite order (byte 0 ↔ byte 3, byte 1 ↔ byte 2).
Precompute a 256-entry table of reversed bytes. Per call: split n into 4 bytes, look up each reversed byte, and shift it to its mirrored byte position.
approaches.complexityReasoning: After the one-time 256-entry table build, each call does 4 mask-lookup-shift operations — constant time. The table is fixed 256 entries → O(256) = O(1) space, amortised across all calls.
approaches.explanation:
Decompose the 32-bit number into four 8-bit bytes. Reverse each byte using a precomputed lookup table, then place the reversed byte into the *opposite* byte position: byte 0 → byte 3, byte 1 → byte 2, and so on. The concatenation of the reversed bytes in swapped order is the fully reversed integer.

**Why reversing bytes then swapping their order works.** Bit reversal is symmetric: the lowest 8 bits of the input become the highest 8 bits of the output, *and* within that group the bits are themselves reversed. So 'reverse each byte' handles the within-byte mirroring and 'swap byte positions' handles the across-byte mirroring. Do both and every bit reaches position `31 - i`.

**Why caching pays off.** A byte has only 256 possible values, so all reversed bytes can be precomputed once. Then each call is four lookups instead of 32 iterations — and across millions of calls that table is built a single time. This directly answers the 'called many times' follow-up.

**Unsigned handling, again.** In Java extract each byte with `(n >>> (8 * i)) & 0xFF` — the unsigned shift plus the `& 0xFF` mask isolate a clean 0–255 byte even from a negative `n`. In Python the same `& 0xFF` extraction works, and the final assembled value is naturally a non-negative 32-bit integer; mask the result with `& 0xFFFFFFFF` if any intermediate widened.
approaches.insight: Trading a fixed 256-entry table for a 8× reduction in per-call work is the classic precompute-and-lookup move. The same divide-into-bytes idea scales: reverse 16-bit halves with a 65536-entry table for even fewer lookups, trading more memory for less time.

dryRun.input: n with bytes [B0, B1, B2, B3] (low to high)
dryRun.intro: Reverse each byte via the table, then send byte i to byte position 3 - i.

steps.note: low byte's reversed bits now occupy the top byte

java.explanation: Build the reversed-byte table ONCE — 256 possible byte values.
Unsigned shift + mask isolates byte i (0-255) even from a negative n.
Reversed byte i goes to mirrored byte position 3 - i.

python.explanation: & 0xFF isolates one byte; n is treated as a 32-bit pattern.
Place the reversed byte at the opposite end.
Clamp to 32 bits so Python's unbounded int stays a valid unsigned 32-bit value.

edgeCases.behavior: Each byte is 0xFF, table[0xFF] = 0xFF, reassembled to 0xFFFFFFFF. Masking keeps Python's result in range.

pitfalls: Reversing the bytes but forgetting to swap their positions (or vice versa) — both transforms are required.
Rebuilding the 256-entry table inside reverseBits on every call — defeats the caching; build it once.
In Python, omitting `& 0xFFFFFFFF` on the result so a widened intermediate yields a value above 2³²−1.

commonMistakes: Using a signed right shift (>>) in Java instead of >>> — corrupts the high bits of negative inputs.
Early-exiting the loop when n reaches 0 — drops leading zeros and misplaces the surviving bits.
In Python, letting the integer grow past 32 bits by not masking shifted intermediates with & 0xFFFFFFFF.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Signed shift corrupts negative inputs (Java)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: `>>` copies the sign bit into the top, so the bits you read back are no longer the original 32-bit pattern. The reversal comes out wrong for any n with the top bit set.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Stopping early when n becomes 0
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Leading zeros of the input must become trailing zeros of the output, which means result still needs the remaining left-shifts. Exiting early leaves the set bits at the wrong positions.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while n:                       # stops as soon as n's high bits are gone
    result = (result << 1) | (n & 1)
    n >>= 1
return result
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for _ in range(32):            # always 32 iterations
    result = (result << 1) | (n & 1)
    n >>= 1
return result

patternNote: Bit-by-bit reversal (consume low, build low). Recognise it for any fixed-width bit-reordering task. The deeper lesson is unsigned discipline: Java needs >>>, Python needs & 0xFFFFFFFF — the same care Sum of Two Integers demands.
